rationale: The book's core claim — that Scripture's pearl figure is the one complete, round, white light of the night sky, the full moon in its office as governor of the appointed times, and thereby the gate of entry (the one-pearl gates of Rev 21:21) — accounts for the specific texture of the supplied texts far better than the strongest common counter (pearl = the kingdom/salvation as supreme value). The counter is a broad thematic label that explains only the generic preciousness in Prov 3:15 and 31:10 and treats Rev 21:21's striking detail — every several gate of ONE pearl — as decorative hyperbole, while leaving Ps 81:3, Prov 7:20, Job 26:9, and Ps 104:19 entirely unaccounted for. The book's chain (peninim recovered as 'pearl' per Strong's; keseh attested as 'full moon' by most translations at Ps 81:3 and Prov 7:20; keseh spelled as kisse'/throne with Job 26:9 holding both senses; the moon appointed for the moedim in Ps 104:19; twelve one-pearl gates matching twelve months of full moons) explains all seven supplied texts as one coherent figure, and even integrates Matt 7:6 (pearls trampled = holy times trodden by the nations, Luke 21:24). No counter-reading I can formulate explains a supplied text that the book's core cannot; the counter's advantage is only its traditional simplicity. However, the secondary elaborations — the full moon as head of the month, the wholesale re-translation of Prov 3 and 31 on unpointed letters, the 'one day not two' grammar of Ps 81:3, and the counterfeit-moon polemic — are not established by the supplied evidence and remain disputed.
book_core_identification: The pearl is the one complete light — the full moon, appointed governor of the moedim (appointed times) — and the one-pearl gates of the New Jerusalem are those appointed times of meeting; the merchant of Matt 13:45-46 buys his entry at the King's gate, not the kingdom itself as an abstract treasure.
book_secondary_elaborations: The full moon (keseh) as the head of the month and the feast-day of Numbers 10:10/28:11, i.e., a revised biblical calendar reckoning

The line-by-line re-translation of Proverbs 3:13-20 and 31:10-31 as portraits of the moon (palms/kaph as the curved light-holding vessel, 'clothed in double,' 'laugheth at the last day' as shachaq, halal as 'shine')
The keseh/kisse' (fulness/throne) wordplay extended through Daniel 7's throne vision and Psalm 89:36-37
The two-moons polemic: the dark conjunction as the counterfeit that 'climbs up some other way' versus the full moon entering the east gate (Ezek 46:1)
Matt 7:6 read as advance notice of the nations trampling the holy times (linked to Luke 21:24; Dan 8:13; Rev 11:2)
Isaiah 33:6 as the weld between the treasure and the times
strongest_counter_interpretation: The pearl symbolizes the kingdom of heaven itself (and by extension salvation, Christ, or the gospel) as the treasure of supreme, surpassing value, worth surrendering everything to obtain (Matt 13:45-46); pearls elsewhere are simply the era's costliest gem, so Prov 3:15/31:10 use them as a generic standard of preciousness, Matt 7:6 uses them for sacred truth, and Rev 21:21's pearl gates are hyperbolic imagery of heavenly glory — enormous single pearls signifying immeasurable worth, with no lunar referent.
counter_core_identification: The pearl = the kingdom of heaven / salvation as the supremely valuable treasure; in all other passages, pearls are simply precious objects standing for value or sacredness, with no single concrete referent.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the pearl has any concrete celestial or calendrical referent: it holds that the pearl in Matt 13:45-46 IS the kingdom (not the gate into it), and that pearls in Prov 3:15, 31:10, and Rev 21:21 are ordinary gemstone imagery of preciousness, so the pearl cannot be the full moon governing appointed times.
counter_case: Matt 13:45-46 frames the parable with 'the kingdom of heaven is like,' and the historically dominant reading takes the pearl as the kingdom/salvation of supreme worth — no lunar mechanics needed

Prov 3:15 and 31:10 are simple value comparisons: wisdom and the virtuous woman exceed the costliest gems; indeed pricing wisdom ABOVE pearls sits awkwardly with identifying wisdom/the bride with the pearl
Ps 81:3, Prov 7:20, Job 26:9, and Ps 104:19 never mention pearls; their relevance is manufactured by the book's own chain (peninim, keseh, kisse'), each link of which is contestable
Peninim may mean coral or rubies rather than pearls in modern lexicography, weakening the founding recovery
Rev 21:21's 'every gate of one pearl' is naturally read as hyperbole of scale and splendor, of a piece with streets of gold and jeweled foundations, not as twelve monthly full moons
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains why Rev 21:21 insists each gate is ONE pearl — one, complete, whole — rather than gates adorned with pearls, and why there are twelve (twelve months of full moons through the twelve gates), a detail the counter must dismiss as hyperbole

Accounts for all seven supplied texts as one coherent figure: peninim under 'rubies,' keseh under 'time appointed' (Ps 81:3) and 'appointed day' (Prov 7:20), the throne/cloud of Job 26:9, and the moon appointed for the moedim (Ps 104:19)

The keseh = full moon reading is independently attested by NKJV, ESV, NASB, JPS at Ps 81:3, and the keseh/kisse' spelling identity at Prov 7:20 is a fact of the consonantal text, with Job 26:9 holding both senses in one verse

Gives Matt 7:6 a mechanically specific reading: what swine do to pearls (trample) is exactly what Scripture says the nations do to holy things and holy times (Rev 11:2; Dan 8:13; Luke 21:24 'until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled')

Resolves the parable's grammar honestly: the kingdom is likened to the MERCHANT, not the pearl, so the pearl as the purchased entry (Isa 33:6, 'wisdom... the stability of thy times... his treasure') fits the syntax the common reading glosses over

The pearl's physical properties (one, round, white, borrowed light, born of waters, standing at a door) converge on exactly one visible object, giving the symbol a concrete, testable referent consistent with the book's demonstrated method (as in the Sower derivation)
counter_explanatory_advantages: Simplicity: requires no multi-step lexical chain (peninim → pearl, keseh → full moon, keseh → throne) and matches the plain devotional force of Matt 13:45-46
Handles Prov 3:15/31:10 without tension: pearls as a generic standard of value that wisdom exceeds, avoiding the book's need to both price the bride 'above pearls' and paint her as the pearl-moon
Aligns with near-universal historical interpretation, patristic through modern, giving it strong external attestation even if that is not itself textual evidence
decisive_sources: Revelation 21:21 — 'every several gate was of one pearl': the singularity and completeness of each gate-pearl, times twelve, is specific data the supreme-value reading leaves unexplained
Psalm 104:19 — 'He appointed the moon for seasons (moedim)': the moon's scriptural office over appointed times, fixing the referent's function

Psalm 81:3 and Proverbs 7:20 — keseh ('fulness/full moon,' KJV 'time appointed'/'day appointed'), attested as 'full moon' by most major translations, tying fullness, the appointed day, and the returning husband together
Job 26:9 — the throne (kisse'/keseh letters) with the cloud spread on its face, binding the throne-spelling to a veiled light

Proverbs 3:15 and 31:10 — peninim under the KJV's 'rubies' (Strong's 'probably a pearl, as round'), placing wisdom and the bride in the pearl's company and supplying the merchant-merchandise thread to Matt 13:45
unresolved_objections: Peninim is rendered coral or rubies by much modern lexicography (cf. the ruddiness of Lam 4:7, not supplied here); the founding recovery rests on Strong's 'probably a pearl' and is not certain

The claim that Ps 81:3 names one day, not two (full moon as the head of the month), and the attendant calendar reckoning, is a radical secondary thesis not established by the supplied texts and deferred by the book itself to another volume

The re-translations of Proverbs 3 and 31 (palms as light-holding vessels, 'clothed in double,' 'laugheth at the last day,' halal as 'shine') rest on unpointed-letter alternate senses; individually attested, but their cumulative lunar portrait is a reading, not a demonstration, as the book concedes
Residual tension between pricing wisdom/the bride ABOVE pearls (Prov 3:15; 31:10) and identifying the bride-portrait with the pearl-moon, mitigated but not eliminated by rendering yaqar as 'bright'
Rev 21:21's one-pearl gates can still be defended as splendor-hyperbole; the book's lunar reading is the better fit for the detail but not the only conceivable one
